title: Ecosystem ecology and current environmental problems
summary: How does energy flow, how does matter cycle, and what disrupts an ecosystem?
cards.0.p: The interaction of living things (biotic) with the nonliving surroundings (abiotic) such as light, water and soil is called an ecosystem. From smallest to largest, the levels are the individual, the population, the community, the ecosystem and the biosphere.
cards.0.key: The individuals of one species in an area form a population. All the populations in that area form the community. An ecosystem also includes the nonliving surroundings.
cards.0.once.soru: Which level do all the carp in a lake form?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: The individuals of one species living in an area form a population.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: A community includes all the species in the lake.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: An ecosystem also includes the nonliving surroundings.
cards.1.p: The place where an organism lives is called its habitat. A habitat is like the organism's address. An ecological niche is the organism's role in the ecosystem, which is like its job. What an organism eats, when it feeds and which resources it uses determine its niche.
cards.1.key: A habitat is an organism's address, and its niche is its job. Competition grows between species whose niches overlap.
cards.1.once.soru: Two birds live in the same tree. One eats insects by day, and the other eats fruit at night. What is different about these birds?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: What they eat and when they feed, in other words their roles, are different.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Both live in the same tree, so they share an address.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: They feed in different ways, so their niches are different too.
cards.2.p: Producers make food from inorganic substances. They do this by photosynthesis or with chemical energy, which is chemosynthesis. Consumers take in ready-made food. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead remains and return minerals to the soil.
cards.2.key: Consumers can be herbivores, carnivores, omnivores or scavengers. Chemosynthetic organisms get energy by oxidizing inorganic substances.
cards.2.etk.soru: Place each organism by its role in the ecosystem.
cards.2.etk.ogeler.1.2: Cyanobacteria carry out photosynthesis, so they are producers.
cards.2.etk.ogeler.2.2: It makes food from inorganic substances by chemosynthesis, so it is a producer.
cards.2.etk.ogeler.6.2: A vulture is a scavenger. It eats dead animals, so it is a consumer. The organisms that break dead remains down all the way to minerals are the decomposers.
cards.2.once.soru: In a forest, which organisms turn dead leaves into minerals?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Decay bacteria and fungi break down dead remains.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: Producers make food. They do not break down dead remains.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Scavengers eat dead animals, but the ones that break them down to minerals are the decomposers.
cards.3.p: A food chain shows how food and energy pass from one organism to the next. Each link in the chain is called a trophic level. When chains connect to each other, they form a food web.
cards.3.key: The more complex a food web gets, the more stable the ecosystem usually is.
cards.3.once.soru: In a chain of grass, grasshopper and frog, what do the arrows show?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: An arrow is drawn from the organism that is eaten to the one that eats it. Energy passes in that direction too.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The arrow is drawn from the eaten to the eater, not from predator to prey.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: The arrows have nothing to do with the size of the organisms.
cards.4.p: Energy enters an ecosystem as sunlight. At each level, most of the energy is lost as heat through respiration. Only about 10% passes to the next level up. So energy flows in one direction, while matter cycles.
cards.4.svg#0: ≈ 90% lost at each level (respiration heat, waste)
cards.4.key: Energy flows, and matter cycles. The 10% is an average. The real share is usually between 5% and 20%.
cards.4.etk.soru: Change the energy entering the producer and the level. About 10% passes to each level.
cards.5.p: The energy pyramid you just explored is always upright. A pyramid of numbers, however, can be inverted. For example, thousands of caterpillars can live on one tree. A biomass pyramid can also be inverted in the ocean.
cards.5.key: In the ocean, fast-growing phytoplankton can have less mass at any one moment than zooplankton. Energy drops at every level, so there are no more than 4-5 levels.
cards.6.p: Substances that the body has trouble getting rid of, such as DDT and mercury, build up in tissues. Each consumer eats many prey, so the concentration of these substances multiplies going up the chain. This is called biomagnification. Top consumers are harmed the most.
cards.6.svg#12: water → bird: about 8 million times higher
cards.6.key: Going up the food chain, energy decreases but poison increases. DDT thinned the eggshells of birds of prey. Mercury poisoned people in Minamata.
cards.7.p: Matter moves through an ecosystem in cycles. The water cycle runs through evaporation, transpiration from leaves, condensation and precipitation. In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis takes up CO2. Respiration, decomposition and burning return CO2 to the air.
cards.7.key: Fossil fuels hold the carbon of ancient organisms, and burning them raises the CO₂ in the air. Oceans and forests are the largest carbon stores.
cards.8.p: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium turn N2 from the air into ammonia. Nitrification turns ammonia into nitrate, and denitrification turns nitrate back into N2. The phosphorus cycle has no gas stage.
cards.8.key: Decomposers turn the nitrogen in dead organisms into ammonia. This is called ammonification. Plants take up nitrogen mostly as nitrate. Phosphorus moves from rocks into the soil, and from there into living things.
cards.9.p: When fossil fuels burn, SO2 and nitrogen oxides are released into the air. These gases combine with moisture to form acids, and acid rain forms. Acid rain harms lakes, soil and forests, and it wears away marble.
cards.9.svg#1: fossil fuels: SO₂, NOₓ, CO, particles
cards.9.svg#3: H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ form in the air
cards.9.key: Normal rain is also slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6), but acid rain has a lower pH. Waste, fertilizers and pesticides also pollute water and soil.
cards.9.once.soru: What is the main source of acid rain?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The SO₂ and nitrogen oxides released when coal and oil burn combine with moisture to form acids.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Ozone thinning is about UV rays, not acid.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Photosynthesis takes up CO₂. It does not produce acid.
cards.10.h: The greenhouse effect, climate and ozone
cards.10.p: The greenhouse effect is a natural process. CO2, methane and water vapor trap heat. When these gases increase, climate change begins. Ozone thinning is a separate problem. CFC gases weaken the ozone layer that protects against UV rays.
cards.10.key: Fossil fuels and deforestation increase greenhouse gases. Glaciers melt and sea level rises. Ozone thinning is not the cause of global warming.
cards.10.once.soru: What would Earth be like with no greenhouse effect at all?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: If the gases did not trap heat, Earth's average temperature would be about −18 °C.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Greenhouse gases trap heat. Without them, Earth would cool down.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The greenhouse effect is a natural process and is needed for life.
cards.11.p: The eutrophication you just saw is started by the nitrogen and phosphorus in fertilizer. When plant cover disappears, soil is carried away by water and wind. This is called erosion. Habitat loss and overhunting reduce biodiversity.
cards.11.key: Invasive species also reduce biodiversity. They spread quickly because they have no natural enemies in their new home. The lionfish in the Mediterranean is an example.
cards.12.p: Species that naturally live only in one particular region are called endemic species. If an endemic species dies out in that region, it is gone from the world. About 80% of the plant species in Madagascar are endemic. Lemurs also live only on this island.
cards.12.key: Islands and high mountains isolate species, so they have many endemic species. The wild ancestors of wheat and chickpeas live in the Fertile Crescent.
cards.12.once.soru: Galápagos giant tortoises live only on those islands. What are such species called?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: An endemic species naturally lives only in one particular region.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: An invasive species arrives in a new place and spreads quickly.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: Pioneer species are the first to settle in a bare area.
cards.13.p: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without using up the options of future generations. The ecological footprint is the productive area needed for the resources we use and the waste we make. A smaller footprint is better.
cards.13.key: The main solutions are recycling, renewable energy, public transport, protected areas and international agreements.
cards.13.once.soru: Which of these shrinks the ecological footprint?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: Public transport cuts fuel use and emissions per person.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: The more we consume, the bigger the ecological footprint.
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: The more waste there is, the bigger the ecological footprint.
cards.14.p: Waste management starts with preventing waste. We need to consume less and reuse things. The waste that remains is sorted at the source and goes to recycling, compost or the battery bin. A landfill is the last option.
cards.14.svg#5: top to bottom: best to last
cards.14.svg#6: sort at the source: paper · plastic · glass · metal · batteries
cards.14.key: The right order is prevent, reuse and recycle. Burying is the last resort.
cards.14.once.soru: What is the first choice in waste management?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The best waste is the waste that never forms.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: Recycling is good, but it comes after preventing waste.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: Burying waste is the last resort.
cards.15.p:
• An ecosystem is made of living things and the nonliving surroundings.
• Energy flows in one direction, and only about 10% passes to each level.
• Water, carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus move in cycles.
• Poisons build up going up the food chain.
• The answer to pollution, climate change and habitat loss is sustainability.
quiz.0.q: Put in order how a nitrogen atom moves from the air to a plant and back to the soil.
quiz.0.e: Bacteria fix N₂ into ammonia, and nitrifying bacteria turn ammonia into nitrate. The plant takes up nitrate with its roots and builds it into its proteins. When the plant dies, decomposers turn the nitrogen back into ammonia. This is called ammonification.
quiz.1.q: In a food chain, the producers store 50,000 kJ of energy. By the 10% rule, about how many kJ reach the secondary consumers?
quiz.1.e: 50,000 × 0.1 = 5,000 kJ passes to the primary consumers. Then 5,000 × 0.1 = 500 kJ passes to the secondary consumers.
quiz.2.q: Match each environmental problem with its main cause.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.1: SO₂ and NOₓ released into the air
quiz.2.e: SO₂ and nitrogen oxides form acids with moisture and cause acid rain. CFCs thin the ozone layer. Nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizer cause eutrophication, rising greenhouse gases cause climate change and loss of plant cover causes erosion.
quiz.3.q: Which of the following statements is true?
quiz.3.o.0: An energy pyramid is never inverted.
quiz.3.o.1: Ozone thinning is the main cause of global warming.
quiz.3.o.2: Like matter, energy cycles through an ecosystem.
quiz.3.o.3: Scavengers such as vultures are decomposers.
quiz.3.e: Energy is lost as heat at every level. So the energy of a higher level can never be greater than that of the level below. The other options are common misconceptions.
quiz.3.y.1: Ozone thinning leads to more UV rays. The main cause of global warming is greenhouse gases.
quiz.3.y.2: Matter cycles, but energy flows in one direction and is lost as heat at every level.
quiz.3.y.3: A vulture is a consumer that tears up and eats carcasses. The decomposers are bacteria and fungi.
A:baslik: Ecosystem ecology and current environmental problems
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Follow energy level by level, track the poison and play through the cycles.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The grass in a meadow stored 10,000 kJ of energy. A grasshopper eats the grass, a frog eats the grasshopper, a snake eats the frog and an eagle eats the snake. Move up the chain and find the level where the energy drops to 100 kJ.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: Only 100 kJ reached the frog, the secondary consumer. At each level, most of the energy is lost as heat through respiration, and some is not digested. On average, only about 10% passes to the next level up. That is why chains are no longer than 4-5 links.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Stacking the levels from bottom to top gives a pyramid. The shape of the pyramid can change depending on what is measured. Switch between the three pyramids.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: Which pyramid is never inverted under any conditions?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Thousands of caterpillars can live on a single tree. Look at pyramid 2.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In the ocean, fast-growing phytoplankton can have less mass at any one moment than zooplankton. Look at pyramid 3.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Each level gets less energy than the one below, because some energy is lost as heat along the way. That is why the energy pyramid is always upright.
A:adimlar.2.metin: A very small amount of DDT got into a lake. DDT is hard for the body to get rid of. Make a guess before you play the chain.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Where is the DDT concentration highest?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The DDT concentration is lowest in the water. The real buildup happens in living tissues.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Plankton builds up much more DDT than the water, but the animals that eat it collect even more.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The concentration multiplies at each level. From 0.000003 ppm in the water, it rises to about 25 ppm in the heron, about 8 million times higher.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Energy flows, and matter cycles. Carbon moves between the CO₂ in the air and living things. Turn on fossil fuel burning, then turn off the decomposers and see what changes.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What is the main process that takes CO₂ from the air and builds it into organic matter?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Respiration breaks down organic matter and returns CO₂ to the air.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Plants and algae build CO₂ into organic matter by photosynthesis. When you turn off the decomposers, carbon builds up in dead matter and does not return to the air.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Burning releases carbon into the air as CO₂. As fossil fuels burn, the CO₂ in the air rises.
A:adimlar.4.metin: About 78% of the air is nitrogen (N₂), but plants cannot use this nitrogen directly. Make a guess before you play the cycle.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: How does N₂ from the air reach a plant?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Even if N₂ enters through the stomata, the plant cannot use it, because the triple bond in the molecule is very strong.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Bacteria turn N₂ first into ammonia, then into nitrate, which the plant can take up with its roots. You will see the names of these steps on the next card.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Lightning also fixes nitrogen, but only a very small part. Bacteria fix most of the nitrogen.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Fertilizer from fields is washing into a lake. The fertilizer contains nitrogen and phosphorus. Guess what will happen, then watch.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: What is the real cause of the oxygen drop that kills the fish?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Living algae make oxygen by photosynthesis during the day. The real consumer is something else.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Fertilizer does not use up oxygen directly. It feeds the algae.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Fertilizer makes the algae multiply too much, and then the algae die and sink. The bacteria that decompose them multiply and use up the water's oxygen through respiration. The fish die. This is called eutrophication.
A:kapanis.0: An ecosystem is made of living things (biotic) and the nonliving surroundings (abiotic).
A:kapanis.1: Energy flows in one direction, and on average only about 10% passes to each level. An energy pyramid is never inverted.
A:kapanis.2: Poisons such as DDT and mercury build up going up the chain. Top consumers are harmed the most.
A:kapanis.3: Matter cycles. Photosynthesis takes up CO₂. Respiration, decomposition and burning give it back. Bacteria fix nitrogen, convert it and return it to the air.
A:kapanis.4: When fertilizer washes into a lake, algae multiply. The bacteria that decompose dead algae use up the oxygen. This is called eutrophication.
